title: Pine Script is a genuinely hostile language, and thats most of why AI keeps handing you broken indicators
author: person-person12
selftext:
**Pine Script looks like the friendliest language in trading and it is one of the most irritating ones to actually write.**

For anybody who doesnt code, quick version. Pine is the language TradingView uses for indicators and strategies. If you want an alert or a line on your chart that nobody has already built for you, Pine is the only door in. It reads like Python from across the room, indentation instead of curly braces and short readable function names. That resemblance is most of the reason people get hurt, because **it does not behave anything like Python once it actually runs.**

The thing that catches everyone first is that a Pine script is not a program that runs top to bottom one time. **It runs top to bottom once per candle, and then again on the next one,** a few thousand times across your chart history. Your variables get wiped and rebuilt on every one of those passes unless you specifically tell them not to with `var`. So the counter you wrote the obvious way sits at 1 forever and you sit there rereading four lines of code that are not wrong. Nothing you learned in any other language warns you about that.

**-----**

**The compile loop is what actually makes it miserable.** Pine only runs inside TradingView. There is no way to run it on your own machine, and nothing you can point at your own data offline. Its like a car that only starts in the dealership lot. You can sit in your driveway reading the manual as long as you want, the key only turns when youre standing on their pavement.

So the entire workflow for every mistake is paste, click, read one red line, guess, paste again.

Here are the errors people actually hit.

**Undeclared identifier.** The most common one by a distance. In current Pine most built ins live behind a namespace, so `sma(close, 14)` is not a thing and `ta.sma(close, 14)` is, `security()` is now `request.security()`, and a whole pile of others moved under `math.` and `str.`. The error does not tell you any of that. It says the name doesnt exist, which is true and useless. And it fires for several unrelated reasons: Pine is case sensitive so `myVar` and `myvar` are two different names, a variable declared inside an `if` block does not exist outside that block, and referencing anything before the line that declares it. One message, four different causes, no hint which one you hit.

**End of line without continuation.** This one is genuinely indefensible. If a statement wraps onto a second line, the continuation has to be indented by a number of spaces that is **not a multiple of four.** Five, six or seven spaces compile fine. Eight does not, because eight reads as two indent levels and Pine thinks youve opened a new block. Two tabs does not either. **You get punished for lining your code up neatly,** and you cant put a comment inside the wrapped statement while youre at it.

**Type qualifiers.** Every value in Pine carries a hidden qualifier: const, then input, then simple, then series, weakest to strongest. Anywhere that wants a `simple int` will happily take something weaker and will flatly refuse a `series int`. In practice that means a length that changes as the chart moves cannot be handed to a function that expects a fixed one, and **the error message reads backwards to how most people think about types,** so the instinct is to go make the value more dynamic, which is the opposite of the fix.

**Scope rules on the drawing functions.** `plot()` and `bgcolor()` have to sit at the top level of the script. Wrapping one in an `if` is the first instinct any programmer has and it is a scope error. Conditional drawing gets done by feeding the condition into the value instead, which is not obvious and is not what the error says.

**And the language keeps moving under you.** v6 deleted the whole `strategy.risk.*` namespace. The old single `input()` got split into `input.int()` and `input.float()` and the parameter names changed with it. Variables that can be `na` on the first candle now want a typed declaration like `float stop = na`. Working v5 code from two years ago does not compile today.

On top of all that it executes on TradingView's servers, so you are also inside hard caps: 40 `request.security()` calls per script, 1000 variables per scope, and a two minute ceiling on compile time.

**The fair part,** because they do deserve it. The v6 namespaces really are better organised than the flat soup they replaced, the reference manual does document every built in, and the Pine Logs pane is real debugging that did not exist a few years ago. None of it helps the person who indented eight spaces.

**-----**

**Why the AI tools keep failing at this specifically**

The reasons compound, and once you see them the failure stops looking random.

**The public corpus is old.** Most Pine on the internet is v4 and v5, so a general model has read far more of that than v6 and will confidently write v5 syntax underneath a `//@version=6` header. Then it hands you an undeclared identifier error for the exact same reason a beginner gets one.

**There is no feedback loop.** A model writing Python can run the file, read the traceback and fix itself before you ever see it. Pine cannot be executed anywhere except TradingView, so a general chatbot is writing completely blind and has no idea its output failed. **You end up doing the checking yourself.** You copy the red text back into the chat, it apologises, it rewrites the whole file, and now line 40 broke instead.

**A lot of the good Pine is closed.** A large share of the strongest scripts on TradingView are invite only or protected, so the source was never public to learn from in the first place.

And the indentation rule is simply not derivable from general programming knowledge. Nobody guesses "not a multiple of four" from first principles.

However, some models like Agenticks' AlgoAgent and LuxAlgo's Quant do make it workable for somebody who doesnt code to turn an idea into a real indicator. Everything above is the reason those had to be built for this one language specifically, instead of being one more thing a general model is already fine at. Both of them check the script against the actual v6 rules and repair it before you ever see it, which is the piece a plain chat window structurally cannot do. LuxAlgo documents that part publicly. I work on the other one, so treat that as disclosure, and im not going to sit here describing our internals.

**-----**

**For anyone who writes Pine by hand, whats the error thats eaten the most of your time?** Im curious whether undeclared identifier is genuinely number one or whether thats just my own experience talking.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
The per bar rebuild is the one that costs people a day of their life, but the more expensive trap is that the same script does not behave the same on history as it does live. On historical bars every bar is already closed. In realtime the last bar is still moving, so anything that reads the current bar gives one answer while it forms and another once it closes.

That is why an AI written indicator can look perfect when you scroll back through the chart and be wrong the moment you trade it. The split is not visible in the source, so the model has no way to warn you about it.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Completely agree, repainting is the one that actually costs money. Anything reading the close of the live candle needs a **confirmed candle check** or a [1] offset. A higher timeframe request with lookahead on and no offset leaks that close straight into history too, which is why it passes the scroll back test.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Scroll back can't catch it by construction: on a historical bar the live close is the final close. Replay or forward paper is the only thing that separates the two.

Between the fixes, [1] costs you a bar while barstate.isconfirmed keeps the signal on its own bar and just fires at close. Which do you use for HTF entries?

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body:
Yea isconfirmed is what I use on the chart timeframe, but it doesnt help much on the HTF side because it confirms the chart candle closed, not the higher timeframe candle. The request.security value keeps moving until that HTF candle actually finishes.

For HTF entries I pull **close[1] with lookahead on** so the value is the last finished HTF candle and never changes, then gate the entry on isconfirmed as well. It costs one HTF candle of delay, and replay and forward paper line up with what the history showed.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
close[1] with lookahead on is the correct pair. What still bites is an HTF that isn't an even multiple of the chart timeframe, so the finished bar repeats across a varying number of chart bars and entry timing drifts without anything repainting.

Do you diff live collected history against a fresh reload?

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: I havent done a systematic live-versus-reload diff yet. Ive been comparing replay with forward paper, which would miss exactly the uneven-multiple drift youre describing. Logging the live signal timestamp and the timestamp of the higher timeframe candle, then diffing both after a clean reload, is the right test here, so this is a good catch.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
One thing that makes the diff sharper: trigger the reload mid HTF candle rather than right after one closes. A clean reload on a closed boundary can agree perfectly and still hide the drift.

Are you logging the bar index alongside the timestamps, or just the times?

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Yea mid candle is the better test. A reload on a closed boundary is the easiest case for two runs to agree on. I'd log **the time and the candle count together**, since the count shifts with how much history the chart loaded.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Candle count being load dependent is exactly why I stopped using the index for anything durable. Bar open time survives a reload, the count doesn't.

Still worth logging both. When they disagree you know the history window moved under you rather than the signal.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Yea open time is the only thing I key off too, **the index moves the second more history loads** on the chart. Logging both is a good call tbh, it turns a silent drift into something you can actually see in the log.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: yeah the index is only stable within one load, thats the part that bites. we had a level anchored to bar_index that quietly moved every time someone scrolled back far enough to pull more history. do you log open time as an int or the formatted string? the string version burned us on a dst boundary.
